events.excerpt: v2.10.3 is a security and stability release on top of v2.10.2 . It's the public release of v2.10.3-priv , which most validators and major RPC providers already run. No hardfork, no database schema change, no resync required. Nodes can be upgraded one at a time, in any order. Highlights Execution : parallel (BlockSTM V2) balance reads are resolved correctly across a self-destruct boundary ( #2403 ). Shared block caches are size-capped and per-tx code hashes memoized, which lowers importer memory under heavy keccak / ecrecover load. Log counting while tracing no longer copies logs ( #2460 ). Txpool : pending chains stranded behind a head that can't be mined are evicted after txpool.strandedlifetime . Filtered addresses also apply to SetCode (type 4) authorizations. The pool signer is no longer swapped when allow-unprotected-txs is set ( #2464 ). Storage trie preload : segmented BFS queue for the preload, plus optional address-cache persistence across restarts. On a mainnet sentry, preload on restart drops from about 1h25m to about 4s. P2P : static peers stay dialed across jails and full dynamic slots ( #2438 ), and are kept out of the peer dropper. RPC : the execution slot is re-acquired between batch items, and the RPC execution pool request timeout from config is applied. Heimdal
events.headline: v2.10.3

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, My name is Shay, and I’m currently working on my final project for a blockchain course, focusing on how decentralized Arbitrum really is in practice. I’ve been reading about BoLD and found it fascinating that validation on Arbitrum One is now permissionless, with the Arbitrum Foundation stepping in as the first active proposer. There’s one thing I couldn’t find a clear answer to, and I’d really appreciate hearing from people who are closer to it: are there actually independent parties running BoLD validators today? And if someone outside the Foundation wanted to take on the proposer role, what would that realistically involve? Also, as part of my research on Arbitrum’s decentralization, I came across the Security Council’s emergency action following the KelpDAO exploit earlier this year, and it’s been on my mind ever since. On one hand, it seems like exactly the kind of situation the Council was designed for. On the other hand, I keep wondering whether it sets a precedent that quietly shifts the balance away from decentralization. I’d really love to hear how people here see it. Was it a necessary safety net, or a step that deserves more scrutiny? And are there any ongoing DAO discussions about setting clearer boundaries on when and how the Council can step in? I’d be

events.excerpt: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework ( CVE-2026-108398 ) was publicly disclosed prior t
events.headline: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

events.excerpt: Why we’re posting. Proposals that put DAO money into liquidity pools often quote the pool’s fee rate (APR). We want to show, with real numbers, why that rate on its own can’t tell you whether the pool made money, and to suggest three simple questions anyone can ask when they see one. This isn’t about any particular proposal, and nobody paid for it. The short version. A pool’s fee rate only counts the money coming in. It leaves out what you lose when prices move. In our data, that loss took back all of the fees on Ethereum-style chains, and about half of them on Solana. What the fee rate leaves out When you put two tokens into a pool, you earn trading fees. That part is real, and it’s what the fee rate shows. But when one token’s price falls, the pool automatically ends up holding more of that token. So compared with simply keeping your two tokens in a wallet, you lose some money. The fee rate never shows this loss. It can’t go below zero. So we measured both parts together on real pool history: fees earned, minus the loss from price moves , compared with just holding the two tokens. 1. Same period, two very different results. events.excerpt: What's Changed Highlights Faster compilation and diagnostics. A series of optimizations across parsing, semantic analysis and lowering: module discovery (including plugin expansion) is now warmed up in parallel, the red-tree arena is built in place and chunked per item, trait-solving lookup contexts and code-size estimation are memoized, calls that would be inlined are no longer specialized first, and hash containers use foldhash. Diagnostics on large Starknet projects improved by up to ~40%. See Optimizations below. Build-independent Sierra output. The function chosen to carry the withdraw_gas check in a recursive cycle, and the order of impl candidates and impl type bounds, are now determined by a structural order instead of salsa internal ids, so the same program always compiles to the same Sierra regardless of parallel warmup. #10437 #10436 Rustc-style names for generated functions. Closures and loops are named {closure#N} / {loop#N} under their defining function (e.g. test::foo::{closure#0}::{loop#0} ) instead of by source location, keeping Sierra debug names stable across edits. events.excerpt: A 21-property attempt combining Certora Prover, Halmos, Foundry, mutation discrimination, historical regression testing, and deployed-bytecode binding. A special thanks to Certora, Halmos, and Foundry for making these tools available. And thank you to pegaslint and the agentic Closed_Models that made it possible. We performed an independent property_driven assurance campaign against Diamond PAU, including formal verification where tractable , symbolic and concrete production-path analysis, deployed_runtime binding, targeted mutation discrimination, and replay of five (5) historical regression classes. No live Diamond PAU vulnerability was established within the tested scope. Several properties remain explicitly unresolved because the formal models were not trustworthy or tractable enough to support stronger claims. This work is not : a claim that Diamond PAU is vulnerability-free; a universal formal verification of the system; a substitute for future review after code or configuration changes. events.excerpt: Two points from the SIP-045 discussion stuck with me: The reserve is accrual-only in PoX-5 (disbursement only via a new SIP), so bond holders take any coverage shortfall themselves for now. @fluidvoice asked whether a “Growth Bond” (3% floor plus upside) could exist alongside the stable bond, since a fixed 3% may feel short-changed in a bull market. events.excerpt: The Ethereum Foundation has established a dedicated post-quantum research team, and the Strawmap/Lean roadmap targets hash-based signatures across the protocol stack. As the largest single manager of validator signing keys on Ethereum (~9M ETH), Lido’s exposure to quantum-vulnerable BLS keys is proportionally the largest in the ecosystem. This pre-proposal suggests forming a small working group to (1) inventory Lido’s key-management exposure, (2) draft a migration playbook aligned with protocol-layer PQ work, and (3) coordinate with the EF PQ team so that Lido node operators are migration-ready well before any hard fork mandates it. Motivation Ethereum’s consensus layer relies on BLS signatures over BLS12-381, which are not resistant to quantum attacks. While protocol-level migration is an EF/domain concern, the operational burden of key rotation at scale falls on staking infrastructure providers — and no entity carries more of that burden than Lido. Recent developments make early preparation timely: • The EF launched a dedicated post-quantum team (Feb 2026); • EIP-8141 (quantum-resistant accounts) has CFI status for Hegotá; • The Lean roadmap outlines hash-based signatures across consensus within a 3–4 year horizon. events.excerpt: ℹ️ This is not a mandatory upgrade, but we ask all pacific-1 validators and node operators to update to v6.7.1 before the FlatKV migration starts (~17:00 UTC on 9 October 2026, when the migration proposal passes). atlantic-2 has already migrated, so operators there can update at their convenience. There is no governance proposal and no coordinated chain halt for this update. v6.7.1 is a patch release on top of v6.7.0 . It has eight fixes and one removal. Most fixes are for the EVM migration, which moves EVM state from memIAVL to FlatKV. Other fixes make state sync and seid rollback safer. v6.7.1 also removes the deprecated seid export command. 🎯 Who Should Update 🛡️ Validators Requested before the migration on pacific-1 . v6.7.1 fixes data races and rollback problems in the state commit store. 🖥️ RPC, full and archive nodes Requested before the migration on pacific-1 . v6.7.1 also fixes wrong contract nonces in the state store after state sync. 🌐 Networks pacific-1 before the migration starts. atlantic-2 at your convenience. ⏱️ Downtime The node stops only for one restart. There is no coordinated halt. 🔗 Compatibility There are no consensus-breaking changes, and the AppHash does not change.
